real_s3.explanation: The unit responds to dogs and dog-like animals (wolves, dingoes, lesser panda) shown in sharp focus. Sharpness of the main subject is the most reliable and most particular feature: it held on new photos at the 97th percentile. The unit also prefers subjects that fill much of the frame rather than small, distant ones. That size preference is strong but largely shared with similar units. The finer size distinction (more than three quarters vs. a quarter to three quarters) and the preference for no visible horizon or straight lines both weakened below the 95th percentile on new photos. The bias toward subjects facing the camera or right rather than left is shared with similar units.

real_s1.explanation: The unit responds to large, sharply focused close-up views of dogs and dog-like animals such as wolves, dingoes and the lesser panda. It is most active when the animal is in crisp focus, fills much of the frame, is roughly centered and often cut off by the frame, and faces the camera rather than to the left. Preference for sharp over slightly blurry subjects is the only effect that held on new photos at an unusual level, and it is strong for this unit. Similar units share it to some degree. A preference for subjects filling more than three quarters of the frame and for backgrounds without straight lines held in direction on new photos, but not at the 95th percentile. Size versus very small subjects and the facing-direction effects look unusual but are largely shared with similar units or rest on few photos.

real_s2.explanation: The unit fires most on dog and dog-like animals (wolves, dingo, lesser panda) shown sharply in focus. Sharpness of the main subject is the effect that replicated on new photos (row 14), though similar units show it too, so it is not unique to this unit. The unit also seems to prefer large subjects that fill much of the frame over small ones. Row 5 is strong but untested, rests on only 6 small-subject photos, and is partly shared with similar units. The finer split of 'more than three quarters' over 'a quarter to three quarters' (row 6) and the preference for no visible straight lines (row 12) both weakened on new photos (percentiles 92 and 89), so they are suggestive but not reliable. The facing-direction effects (rows 1 and 2) are inconsistent across similar units and were not tested. They may reflect frontal views, but I am not confident in them.

null_s1.explanation: The unit responds to dogs and dog-like animals (wolves, dingo, lesser panda) among its top classes. The most reliable pattern is that it is weaker when the animal faces or points to the left. It is stronger for animals facing right or facing toward or away from the camera. The right-versus-left preference is fairly particular to this unit, since two of the three similar units do not show it. The effects for sharpness, a subject filling more than three quarters of the frame, and a background without straight lines all failed on new photos, and the frame-filling effect even reversed. The preference for large over very small subjects rests on only 6 small-subject photos, so it is too fragile to rely on. All confident rows are untested on new photos.

null_s3.explanation: The unit is most active on close-up dog and dog-like animal photos. None of the three picked claims held up on new photos: sharpness (row 14), no visible straight lines (row 12) and frame-filling size (row 6) all failed, and the size preference even reversed. The one remaining signal that looks particular to this unit is a lower response when the subject faces left than when it faces right. That rule was not tested on new photos, so confidence is modest. The weaker response to left-facing subjects compared with camera-facing ones (row 2) is shared with similar units. The size rows comparing against tiny subjects (rows 4 and 5) rest on only 6 photos and conflict with the failed row 6.

null_s2.explanation: The unit responds to dogs and dog-like animals such as wolves, dingoes and lesser pandas, the classes it is most active on. Within those classes its clearest within-class preference concerns facing direction. It is weaker when the animal faces or points left, and stronger when it faces right or toward/away from the camera (rows 1 and 2). The right-over-left asymmetry (row 1) is not shared by two of the three similar units, so it looks most particular to this unit, though it was not retested on new photos. The unit also prefers a subject that is large rather than tiny in the frame (rows 4 and 5). That preference is largely shared with similar units, and row 5 rests on only 6 small-subject photos. Three finer distinctions failed on 118 new photos: sharpness (row 14), absence of straight lines (row 12), and more-than-three-quarters versus mid-sized subjects (row 6, which reversed). They were likely noise in the first sample, and rows 7, 8 and 13, which are similar weak or small-sample effects, are not trustworthy either.
